# Framework Development and Results {#sec-chapter4}

Twelve months of live ITSM and CMDB records from a regulated Swiss trading institution supply the raw material for this chapter. The indicator values extracted from those records, the normalisation and weighting decisions applied to them, and the TOPSIS scores that result are each documented and justified in the sections below.

## Data Preparation {#sec-dataprep}

The trading IT portfolio includes 108 services. Fifty-three of these are small vendor applications such as trading graphical user interfaces and were excluded from the analysis because they require no significant ongoing activity from the portfolio's IT teams.

From the remaining services, the six with the highest incident and change volumes were selected. These services represent the major services within the portfolio and were chosen because their underlying data is the most complete and therefore best suited to reliable analysis. All selected services are registered as active configuration items and have been in operation for more than 36 months. Service identifiers were replaced with alphanumeric codes before analysis in line with the anonymisation procedure described in @sec-ethics. The dataset contains no team, vendor, or individual identifiers.

### Indicator Extraction and Quality Checks

The five indicators defined in @sec-datasources were extracted from the organisation's ITSM instance and CMDB on 11 June 2026. Only production records were included in the extraction; incidents, changes, and configuration items classified under non-production environments were excluded.

Prior to normalisation, several quality filters were applied to the raw incident data. Incidents sharing a common root cause but recorded as multiple separate tickets, a pattern typical of alarm storms, were consolidated and counted as a single incident to avoid inflating frequency counts. Incidents with an MTTR below 0.1 hours were excluded on the grounds that resolutions at that speed are highly likely to reflect automatic closure following a false alarm or instant recovery rather than genuine remediation effort. To address the upper tail of the MTTR distribution, a 98th percentile cap was applied; incidents exceeding this threshold were excluded as their resolution times are more plausibly attributable to administrative inactivity or elapsed calendar time than to active resolution effort.

All CMDB records were found to be complete. No imputation or worst-case substitution was required.

### Data Limitations {#sec-datalimitations}

The data carry inherent quality limitations that must be acknowledged before interpreting the results. Incident P2/P3/P4 classifications vary across teams, reflecting local triage conventions rather than a uniform severity standard. Patch recency is bounded by CMDB coverage and scanner configuration, so services with incomplete configuration records may appear more current than they are.

Because the organisation does not document CFR directly, it is derived from incident and change records as described in @sec-datasources. This means incident frequency and CFR depend on the accuracy and completeness of the incidents that have been opened. Recording practices vary across teams: some contacts arrive by phone or email and whether these result in a formal ITSM record depends on the discipline of the receiving team. Others are handled as defects or bugs within Jira and never escalated into the ITSM instance. Services where informal handling is common may therefore show lower incident counts and CFR values than their true failure rate warrants, which would systematically compress their priority scores.

These limitations do not invalidate the proxy approach. Scores should be interpreted as ordinal priority signals rather than exact measurements. The sensitivity analysis in @sec-chapter5 tests whether the ranking is robust to the input variation these data quality factors may introduce.

## Indicator Normalisation and Weighting

Each indicator was normalised using vector normalisation, as specified in @sec-frameworkdesign. This removes differences in scale and unit while preserving proportional relationships between values. A service with an unusually high MTTR retains its full distance from lower-performing services in the normalised space, rather than being compressed toward a fixed upper bound. Min-max normalisation was considered and rejected on this basis. @grecoMethodologicalFrameworkComposite2019 recommend vector normalisation for composite indicators precisely because it does not reduce the discriminatory power of extreme observations.

Two weight configurations are applied, as specified in @sec-frameworkdesign. The baseline equal-weight configuration assigns $w_j = 0.20$ to each of the five criteria and serves as the reference case. The differential configuration assigns higher weights to MTTR and CFR, consistent with the design rationale established in @sec-chapter3. The differential weights are $w_{\text{MTTR}} = w_{\text{CFR}} = 0.30$ and $w_{\text{IncFreq}} = w_{\text{Patch}} = w_{\text{UnsupComp}} \approx 0.133$.

| Configuration    | Incident Freq. | MTTR  | CFR   | Patch Recency | Unsup. Comp. Months |
|------------|------------|------------|------------|------------|------------|
| Equal (baseline) | 0.200          | 0.200 | 0.200 | 0.200         | 0.200               |
| Differential     | 0.133          | 0.300 | 0.300 | 0.133         | 0.134               |

## TOPSIS Computation and Rankings {#sec-topsis-results}

The computation follows the TOPSIS formulation specified in @sec-frameworkdesign and was executed using the Python artefact in Appendix A. This process calculates the closeness coefficient $C_i$ for each service based on its Euclidean distance from the ideal solution. A higher $C_i$ indicates that a service is closer to the positive ideal solution, while a lower $C_i$ signals higher technical debt priority. Since the framework is intended to guide prioritisation, the service with the least favourable score receives the highest rank.

@tbl-topsis-results presents the full results under both weight configurations. The table is sorted from highest to lowest debt priority, so rank 1 = highest priority for remediation.

| Service | $S_i^+$ | $S_i^-$ | $C_i$ (equal) | Rank (equal) | $C_i$ (diff.) | Rank (diff.) |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| SVC-03  | 0.2786  | 0.0000  | 0.0000        | 1            | 0.0000        | 1            |
| SVC-01  | 0.2179  | 0.0631  | 0.2245        | 2            | 0.1978        | 2            |
| SVC-05  | 0.0939  | 0.2313  | 0.7112        | 3            | 0.6244        | 3            |
| SVC-02  | 0.0641  | 0.2153  | 0.7707        | 4            | 0.7745        | 4            |
| SVC-04  | 0.0000  | 0.2786  | 1.0000        | 5            | 1.0000        | 5            |

: TOPSIS closeness coefficients and rankings. Higher $C_i$ indicates lower debt priority. {#tbl-topsis-results tbl-colwidths="\[12,12,12,16,14,16,14\]"}

The rankings are fully stable across both weight configurations. All five services occupy identical rank positions under equal and differential weighting, and Kendall's $\tau$ between the two configurations is 1.00. The two configurations differ by up to 16.7 percentage points per criterion, so this absence of rank changes is a substantive rather than an incidental result. It indicates that the relative ordering of services in this portfolio is insensitive to whether MTTR and CFR are elevated above the remaining indicators.

## Interpretation and Discussion {#sec-interpretation}

The framework produces a prioritisation list that maps operational service management data onto a single comparable priority score. SVC-03 occupies the lowest $C_i$ position (rank 5, highest debt priority) under both configurations. It presents the highest incident frequency at 3.1 per month, the highest MTTR at 52.8 hours, the highest CFR at 0.41, the lowest patch recency at 0.38, and the highest unsupported component months at 24.6. This convergent multi-indicator profile points in the same direction across all five dimensions. @hakiDigitalNudgingTechnical2023 define infrastructure lifecycle debt as cumulative months of exposure to unsupported components and identify it as a distinct, measurable debt category in large financial institutions, separate from code-level and vulnerability debt. SVC-03's profile -- combining high operational instability with the largest unsupported component exposure in the portfolio -- is consistent with a service exhibiting the operational consequences associated with this debt category, though the causal direction cannot be established from cross-sectional data alone.

SVC-04 occupies the opposite extreme ($C_i = 1.00$, rank 1, lowest debt priority). It records the lowest values on all four cost indicators and the highest patch recency. Its presence anchors the positive ideal solution against which all other services are measured and provides a concrete reference point for what a well-maintained operational profile looks like in this portfolio.

SVC-01 and SVC-05 present the most analytically substantive profiles. SVC-01 carries elevated values across incident frequency, MTTR, and unsupported component months simultaneously, suggesting that its debt is distributed across both operational and infrastructure dimensions. SVC-05, by contrast, presents a low incident frequency (0.5 per month) and a low CFR (0.07), but an MTTR of 44.2 hours. When failures occur, resolution is slow despite the service appearing stable under normal conditions. This mixed profile illustrates the core advantage of the multi-criteria approach. Sorting by incident frequency alone would place SVC-05 second in the portfolio, missing the recovery penalty embedded in its MTTR. Sorting by patch recency alone would rank it fourth. The TOPSIS score integrates these signals and produces a ranking that reflects each service's combined operational state rather than its performance on any single dimension.

Under the differential weight configuration, SVC-05's MTTR penalty receives greater weight, yet its rank position does not change. This is because SVC-05's MTTR, while high in absolute terms, is not sufficient to displace SVC-02, which combines a markedly lower MTTR with comparably strong patch recency and low unsupported component exposure. The rank boundary between positions two and three is stable under both configurations.

Taken together, the results address RQ1 directly. Technical debt in this trading IT portfolio can be quantified at the service level using ITSM and CMDB data without access to source code. The framework produces a complete, internally consistent, and reproducible ranking through a transparent and documented procedure. Whether these rankings correspond to independently verified assessments of technical debt severity -- the question underlying RQ2 -- cannot be established from the framework output alone and is addressed in @sec-chapter5 through convergent validation against an independent operational metric not used as a framework input.
